t: Extract Kth Character From The Rope Tree
o: A rope tree represents a long string as concatenations stored in a binary tree: leaves hold substrings, internal nodes store lengths. To get the k-th character (1-indexed), walk down from the root: if the left subtree's length ≥ k, descend left; otherwise subtract the left length from k and descend right. At a leaf, answer is leaf.val[k−1]. Examples confirm: root=[10,4,"abcpoe","g","rta"], k=6 → left len 4 < 6, so k=2 on right "rta" → 'b'. Tree size ≤ 1000, so recursion depth is safe.
k: Compare k against node.left.len to choose the descent direction.
Subtract left length when going right; leaf answers val[k-1].

a.i: At each internal node, S[node] = S[left] + S[right], and node.len equals that total. If k fits within the left part, recurse left; else recurse right with adjusted k. Each step discards half the structure, giving logarithmic depth in practice and guaranteed termination at a leaf.
s: If node is a leaf, return node.val[k-1].
If k <= L, recurse into left with same k; else recurse into right with k − L.
a.t: O(h) where h is tree height — one path from root to leaf

a.i: Same logic without recursion: loop until reaching a leaf, adjusting k along the way. Avoids stack overhead and is trivially convertible to other languages.
s: While node.len > 0: compute left length, branch and adjust k.

w: Either version is fine; iterative avoids recursion-depth concerns on skewed trees. Pitfalls: 1-indexed k (use k−1 at the leaf), nodes with only one child (guard null left/right), and trusting node.len instead of computing string lengths (the problem guarantees consistency). Follow-up: support insert/delete efficiently — that's the real-world rope data structure motivation.
